The Fat mouse Steatomys pratensis is a small, nocturnal murid rodent inhabiting the savannas and woodlands of southern and central Africa. In captivity, when maintained at a steady 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], adult individuals achieve a maximum adult body mass of 37.54 grams [Wwi = 37.54 grams], a value that is modest relative to other members of the subfamily Dendromurinae. Basal metabolic rate, assessed via respirometry in post-absorptive animals resting within their thermoneutral zone, averages 18.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 18.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C]. This relatively low metabolic expenditure is consistent with the species’ granivorous diet and its tendency to enter daily torpor during periods of food scarcity, an adaptation that considerably reduces energetic demands. Field studies suggest that this torpor-prone lifestyle may also influence the species’ slow pace of life, a characteristic reflected in several other life-history parameters measured under laboratory conditions.

Under the same thermoneutral regime of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], reproductive parameters for Steatomys pratensis have been documented from captive colonies. Gestation spans 21 days [tg = 21 days], a duration consistent with other small murine rodents, though records indicate that it can extend to as many as 24 days in some pregnancies at a temperature of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C]. Females typically produce between 2 and 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 7 pups per litter], with an average of about 6 litters per year [F_R_i = about 6 litters per year]. The combination of moderate litter size and relatively high annual reproductive frequency suggests a capacity for rapid population turnover under favorable conditions. Neonates are altricial at birth, weighing approximately 1.6 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.6 grams], a value extrapolated from allometric relationships within closely related taxa such as Saccostomus campestris, which suggests a predictable scaling of birth weight relative to adult female size.

Developmental milestones in this species are also tightly linked to thermal conditions. When reared at 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], young reach the time since birth at weaning of 21 days [tx = 21 days], at which point the nursing offspring transition to a diet of solid seeds and insects, achieving a wet weight at weaning of approximately 3.9 grams [Wwx = approximately 3.9 grams]. This rapid pre-weaning growth is typical of small altricial rodents and is supported by the female's rich milk composition. The weaning mass is a critical benchmark, as it marks the onset of nutritional independence and the beginning of the juvenile phase, a period during which individuals must acquire foraging skills while remaining vulnerable to predation. The close correspondence between the weaning age and the gestation length is notable, suggesting a tightly scheduled reproductive cycle that maximizes litter production within the limited breeding season characteristic of this region's unpredictable rainfall patterns.

Sexual maturation in Steatomys pratensis occurs relatively early for a rodent of its size. When maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], males and females become capable of reproduction at a time since birth at puberty of 70 days [tp = 70 days]. This onset of reproductive maturity is fairly rapid, allowing young born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute to later litters within the same year. The relatively short interval from birth to puberty, paired with the modest gestation length, underpins the species’ potential for multi-litter seasons and rapid numerical response to favorable environmental conditions such as post-drought resource pulses. In the wild, however, the actual age at first breeding may be delayed by ecological constraints including competition for burrow sites and the availability of high-quality food resources necessary to support the energetic costs of gestation and lactation.

Longevity data for Steatomys pratensis, collected from captive records under stable conditions at 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years]. This is a surprisingly long lifespan for a rodent of only 37.54 grams [Wwi = 37.54 grams], as most similarly sized murids rarely exceed two to three years. The extended longevity may be linked to the species' capacity for torpor, which reduces cumulative metabolic damage and oxidative stress over the course of its life. In natural populations, mortality from predation and environmental extremes likely truncates this potential considerably, although the physiological capacity for extended survival remains an intriguing characteristic that positions Steatomys pratensis as an outlier among small African rodents in terms of its life-history strategy, combining a relatively high reproductive output with an unusually slow pace of aging.
